questions.stem: The landmark 1992 Earth Summit — at which the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) was signed — was held at:
questions.explanation: The 1992 Earth Summit was held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The UNFCCC (climate), CBD (biodiversity) and the Forest Principles all came out of this summit. Stockholm — 1972, the first major world environment conference (UNEP was created as a follow-up). Johannesburg — 2002 World Summit on Sustainable Development (Rio+10). Rio+20 — Rio again, 2012.

questions.stem: The Kyoto Protocol, which committed developed countries to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions, was adopted in:
questions.explanation: Kyoto Protocol — adopted at COP-3 in December 1997, entered into force in 2005. Mandatory emission-reduction targets only for developed ('Annex I') countries in its first commitment period (2008-12). The US never ratified it. Its successor — the Paris Agreement, adopted at COP-21 in December 2015, involves every country. The 1987 Montreal Protocol is a separate treaty — about ozone-layer-depleting substances, not climate change.

questions.stem: The Paris Agreement of 2015 aims to keep the long-term rise in global average temperature below:

options.option_text: 2°C (with an aspiration of 1.5°C) above pre-industrial levels

questions.explanation: The Paris Agreement (COP-21) aims to limit warming to 'well below 2 °C' and to pursue efforts to keep it to 1.5 °C relative to pre-industrial (1850-1900) temperature. Each country submits NDCs (Nationally Determined Contributions), updated every 5 years. India's updated NDC (2022) — reduce emissions intensity of GDP by 45 % from 2005 level by 2030; 50 % of electricity from non-fossil sources by 2030. Net-zero target — 2070.

questions.stem: The IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) was established in:
questions.explanation: IPCC — set up in 1988 by the World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) and the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) to assess the science of climate change. Its reports (Assessment Reports AR1 to AR6, Special Reports like the 1.5 °C Report) underpin UNFCCC negotiations. Nobel Peace Prize 2007 (shared with Al Gore). Headquartered in Geneva. Does not do original research — synthesises existing science.

questions.stem: The Montreal Protocol (1987) is primarily about the phase-out of substances that deplete:
questions.explanation: Montreal Protocol (1987) — phases out CFCs, halons, carbon tetrachloride etc. Credited as the most successful international environmental treaty; the ozone hole is measurably healing. The Kigali Amendment (2016) added phase-down of HFCs (which do not harm ozone but are potent greenhouse gases). Stockholm Convention (2001) — POPs. UNFCCC/Kyoto/Paris — climate change.

questions.stem: COP-26 (2021), the climate summit that produced the 'Glasgow Climate Pact', was hosted by:
questions.explanation: COP-26 — Glasgow, UK, 2021. India announced 'Panchamrit' (five pillars) — 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030, 50 % of energy from renewables, 1 GT emission cuts, intensity -45 %, net-zero by 2070. COP-27 — Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt (2022) — Loss-and-Damage fund agreed. COP-28 — Dubai, UAE (2023) — first global stocktake + 'transitioning away from fossil fuels' in the agreed text.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most abundant human-generated greenhouse gas by volume in Earth's atmosphere?
questions.explanation: CO₂ — dominant human-emitted greenhouse gas, ~420 ppm in 2024 (pre-industrial ~280 ppm). Methane — more potent per molecule (about 25× over 100 years) but at much lower concentration (~1,900 ppb). N₂O, SF₆ and HFCs are tiny fractions but can be long-lived and potent. Water vapour is the largest natural GHG but responds to temperature rather than driving it directly.
